opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so what's really exciting is that confidential computing has finally moved from the CPU to the GPU. For a long time we had trusted execution environments on the CPU side, things like Intel SGX and then TDX, where you can run code in an enclave and the operator of the machine can't see what's happening inside. But for AI that wasn't enough, because all the interesting computation happens on the GPU. With Nvidia's newer generations, starting with Hopper and continuing with Blackwell, you can now have the GPU itself run in confidential mode. The memory is encrypted, the channel between the CPU enclave and the GPU is encrypted, and the hardware can produce an attestation saying exactly what code and which model is running.

That changes the trust model for AI. Right now, when you send a query to a model provider, you're trusting that company not to look at your data, log it, or train on it. With confidential computing you don't have to trust the operator. You verify cryptographically that your data went into a specific environment, was processed by a specific model, and nobody else, not the cloud provider and not the person who owns the hardware, could see it.

For us, coming from the NEAR and user-owned AI perspective, that's the missing piece. It means you can have a decentralized network of GPU providers, where you don't know or trust who's running the machines, and still get privacy guarantees comparable to running on your own hardware. And it lets you do things like private inference on personal data, or even fine-tuning on sensitive data, where the data owner and the model owner both keep their assets protected.

It's not perfect. There's overhead, there have been side-channel attacks on enclaves historically, and you're ultimately trusting the hardware vendors and their attestation infrastructure. But compared to "just trust the company with your data," it's a massive step forward, and I think it's going to become foundational for how people interact with AI that knows a lot about them.

r001.rationale: The response says the operator and the person who owns the hardware cannot see the computation inside the confidential environment, and describes this for Intel CPUs and Nvidia GPUs.

r002.rationale: It says an attestation identifies the code and model, and that the requester can verify their data was processed there. It does not say the certificate attests that the returned result came from running the submitted data through that computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been excited about for a while. The way I think about it is that confidential computing is really the missing piece for making AI actually trustworthy and user-owned, and the fact that Nvidia and Intel now ship it in hardware changes what's possible.

So the basic idea is that the chip itself creates an isolated environment, a trusted execution environment, where the memory is encrypted and even the operator of the machine, the cloud provider, whoever has root on the box, can't see what's happening inside. And critically, the hardware can produce an attestation, a cryptographic proof, that says "this exact code is running on this exact chip in this isolated mode." Intel had this for CPUs for a while with SGX and now TDX, but the thing that really unlocked it for AI is Nvidia bringing it to the H100 and the newer GPUs. Because before that, you could run a confidential CPU workload, but the moment you needed a GPU for inference or training, all your data left the enclave and you were back to just trusting whoever runs the data center.

What I find interesting is what that enables. Right now, when you send a prompt to a model API, you're trusting the company on a bunch of things. That they're not logging your data, that they're actually running the model they say they're running, that nobody's modified the system prompt, that the weights haven't been swapped. There's no way to verify any of it. With confidential computing you can verify it. You get a proof that the model is what it claims to be and that your data was processed in a way that the provider couldn't even see. And that works in both directions, the model owner can also protect their weights from the people running the hardware.

And then, for us at NEAR, the piece I really care about is combining that with blockchain. Because the attestation gives you a verifiable statement, but you need somewhere to record it and to coordinate around it. So you can imagine agents that run inside these enclaves, that hold keys, that transact, and users can actually verify what code is acting on their behalf. That's a very different world from "trust us." That's the thing that got me interested, it's a path toward AI that's private and verifiable without having to run everything on your own laptop.

The caveats are real though. The ecosystem is still early, there have been side-channel attacks against these systems historically, and you're ultimately still trusting Intel and Nvidia as hardware manufacturers. So it's not a silver bullet, but it moves the trust from a company's policy document to a much smaller and more auditable surface, and that's a big improvement.

r001.rationale: It says the isolated environment prevents the machine operator, cloud provider, or anyone with root access from seeing what happens inside.

r002.rationale: It describes attesting that specific code is running on a specific chip and that data was processed, but does not clearly say the attestation certifies that the returned result came from applying the specified computation to the submitted data.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is the ability to compute on private data while giving people guarantees about what’s actually running. Usually, if you send your data to somebody’s server, you’re trusting that operator. With confidential computing, the idea is that the hardware isolates the computation, and you can verify that it’s running the code you expected.

For AI, that opens up an interesting possibility: you could use a model with sensitive personal or business information without exposing that information to the company operating the machine. And having that capability on GPUs matters because that’s where much of the AI computation happens.

You’re still making trust assumptions about the hardware and its implementation. But it gives us another building block for systems where you don’t have to hand over control of your data just to get something useful done.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that you can run computation on someone else’s hardware without giving the operator access to the data being processed. With confidential computing, the hardware provides an isolated environment, and attestation gives you a way to verify what code is running before you send it sensitive information.

For AI, that’s particularly useful. You might want to use a powerful model with your private documents or business data, but you don’t necessarily want the infrastructure provider to see those inputs. Having protection across both the CPU and GPU makes that much more practical.

There are still trust assumptions—you’re trusting the hardware vendor and the implementation—but it creates an interesting path toward services where privacy is enforced technically, rather than just promised in a policy.

r001.rationale: It says confidential computing lets you compute on someone else’s hardware without the operator accessing the data, using an isolated environment, and mentions protection across CPU and GPU.

r002.rationale: It describes attestation as verifying which code is running before sending data, but does not say a certificate verifies that the returned result came from applying the specified computation to the submitted data.
